paragraphs.text:
On Himself, on Returning from the Country after the Affair of Maximus.

1. I longed for you, my children, and I was longed for in equal measure. I am convinced of it, and if I must add an oath to my word: "Yes, by the boast in you, brothers, that I have in Christ Jesus our Lord." For the Holy Spirit has made this oath for me, the Spirit by whom we were moved toward you, so that we might prepare for the Lord a people of his own. [?] Believe me: I am as sure of my own feelings as I am insistent about yours. And there is nothing surprising in that. For those who share the Spirit share the feeling too, and those whose experience is equal have equal faith. What someone has not felt himself he will not believe of another; but one who has felt it is readier to assent, an invisible witness to an invisible feeling, a familiar mirror of another's form. That is why I could not bear to stay away from you any longer, although I was quite annoyed and weighed down by things here. It was not only what cities bring: crowds, tumults, [?] marketplaces, theatres, gluttony, insolence, people who carry off and are carried off, who fine and are fined, who mourn and are mourned, who weep, rejoice, marry, bury, who are praised and who are slandered, the raw material of vice, the seething of the world, its sudden reversals, as in a Euripus or in the winds. It was also these things, more solemn and honourable, those around the bema, the people and the shepherds [?].

I mean around the holy table, where we seem to hold the first place and are reckoned among those who draw near to God. I fear that we draw near unworthily, and, like stubble before fire, cannot bear the fire.

2. However, I have come back to you. I was driven away by force, but I have hurried back not by force, rather very eagerly, and "on willing feet," as the saying goes, with the Spirit [?] leading me like a stream, which is forced when it goes uphill but rushes when it goes downhill. Truly, to those sick with longing a single day is a whole human life. Jacob's case seems to me [?] to have been different. He served Laban the Syrian fourteen years for the two maidens and did not grow weary: "All the days," it says, "were to him as one day, because he loved them." Perhaps that was because the one he longed for was before his eyes, or because toil is light to love, even if delay brings its pain. In the same way, what lies ready at hand dulls desire, as one of those before us said. At any rate, while I was with you I scarcely felt the emotion, but once I was separated from you I came to know longing, that sweet tyrant. There is nothing new in this. A herdsman grieves so much over a calf that has strayed from the herd, a shepherd over a sheep missing from his flock, a bird over the nest it left for a little while, that the herdsmen and shepherds take their pipes, climb to some lookout, fill the reeds with their dejection and call back the strays as though they had reason. If the strays obey, they rejoice over them more than over all the rest together, whom they did not worry about. The bird, chirping, darts back to its nest, falls on its chirping nestlings and covers them with its wings. How much more, then, must rational flocks mean to a skilful shepherd, especially ones for whom he once faced danger, since that too adds to the affection! So I fear the savage wolves, lest they watch for our darkness and tear the flock with [?] words,

since they wait for unguarded moments, unable to prevail openly. I fear robbers and thieves, lest they climb over the fold and either plunder shamelessly or steal by deceit, "to kill and to slaughter and to destroy," "seizing prey, devouring souls," as one of the prophets said. I fear the side door, lest one of those who were ours only yesterday or the day before find it unlocked, come in as one of our own, and then plot against us as a stranger. For the schemes of the one who works such things are many and varied, and nobody is so masterly a builder of any intricate thing as the adversary is a sophist of wickedness. And I already fear dogs too, who force their way into being shepherds and, strangest of all, have brought nothing to the shepherd's craft except cutting off the hair they cultivated so badly. They have neither stayed dogs nor become shepherds; they only tear apart, scatter and undo the labour of others. For destroying is always easier than preserving. A man is born with labour, says Job; a ship is built and a house put together with labour; but anyone who wishes can kill, tear down or set on fire. So let those who set the dogs on the flock not be proud even now. They cannot name a single sheep they have brought in or saved, for they have not learned to do good, having practised wickedness. If they trouble the flock, so can a small squall, so can a slight disease, so can a single wild beast that falls on it all at once. Let those who glory in their own shame stop, then. Let them cease from their wickedness, if they can, and worship and fall down and weep before the Lord who made them, and let as many as are not wholly incurable be joined to the flock.

"Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is made to stumble, and I do not burn," or am not anxious? "For I seek not what is yours, but you." And again: "I was scorched by the heat of the day and pinched by the frost of the night." These are the words of a patriarch who was a shepherd, whose sheep were marked and had learned to conceive at the watering troughs there. This, then, is how I have come back to you, and why, and how things stand. Now that I have come, let us give each other an account of what we have achieved in the meantime. For it is good to believe that we will be asked to account not only for every word and deed but for every season, even for the briefest and slightest hour. You report your work to me, and I will set before you the reflections I pursued in quiet, keeping my own company.

5. What contemplation of lofty things have you either received from me and kept, or produced yourselves, concerning theology or the other doctrines I have so often and so fully entrusted to you? For I seek not only the loan but the interest, not only the talent but the trading. Let no one hide and bury what was entrusted to him and then slander the one who entrusted it as harsh and greedy for what belongs to others. What praiseworthy deed have you borne as fruit, whether one that not even your left hand knows, or one that lets your light shine before men? Then the tree will be known by its fruit and the teacher made known through his disciples, and someone among those who watch our affairs (and they are many, some with goodwill, some out of curiosity) may say, "Truly God is among you," not only soundly preached but also worshipped. For just as no deed is approved without faith (since many practise the good for the sake of reputation, or because they are made that way by nature), so too faith without works is dead. Let no one deceive you with the empty words of those who readily allow everything for the sake of one thing, impiety in doctrine, and pay a base wage for a base business. Show your faith, then, by your works; show the fertility of your soil, whether we have sown in vain, whether there is a sheaf among you strong enough to make flour and worthy of the barns, so that we may cultivate you more eagerly. Who bears fruit a hundredfold, who sixtyfold, who at least thirtyfold? Or who, going the other way, has advanced from thirty to sixty (for the Gospels give us this order too) and ended at a hundred? Then, advancing like Isaac, he may become great, going from strength to strength, singing the Songs of Ascents and setting ascents in his heart.

6. I seek the fruit that increases to your credit. The gain is yours, not mine; yet it is ours too, because it is yours, since the benefit is reflected back from you to us, as light is in reflections. Have you fed the poor? Have you shown hospitality? Have you washed the feet of the saints? While indulging the belly that is to be destroyed (let that be allowed), have you also delighted in the commandments? For there is no better delight than this, nor any more lasting, for those who wish to delight. Have you, as far as you could, given relief to any of those who serve at the altar and are honourably poor (allow me to say this too), so that they may wait on the altar with fewer distractions and, sharing in your goods, give theirs in return? For it is shameful that we should have to ask for these things and that you should fail to provide them. I have not given this advice so that it may be done for me (for I would rather die than have my boast made empty, and my preaching of the Gospel lose its reward by my reaping its fruits here; preaching the Gospel is a necessity, but the honour lies in doing it free of charge). I have given it so that you may learn to do good to Christ by doing good even to some of the little ones. For just as he became everything that I am, except sin, for my sake, so he also takes on himself even the least of what is mine: if you share a roof or clothing, if you visit someone in prison, if you look in on someone who is ill, or at the very least if you cool with a single cup of cold water the tongue of someone in distress, as the rich man suffering in the flame begged of Lazarus the poor man. In return for his luxury here, and for ignoring Lazarus hungry and covered in sores, he received this: to need Lazarus there and not obtain

7. These, then, are the things we ask of you. And I know that you are not ashamed when we ask you for an account, nor when the last day does so, the day into which all our affairs are gathered, according to [?]

what was said: "And I am coming to gather your counsels and your deeds"; and, "Behold the man, and his work, and his reward with him." Our part is to bring you what we have gathered in solitude. For Elijah gladly pursued philosophy on Carmel, and John in the desert; and Jesus himself mostly gave his deeds to the crowds but his prayers to leisure and solitary places. What law was he laying down? I think it was that we must also keep some quiet, so as to converse with God untroubled and draw the mind back a little from the things that wander. He himself had no need of withdrawal, for, being God and filling all things, he had nowhere to withdraw into. He did it so that we might learn both the time for action and the time for a higher leisure. What, then, has my solitude produced? For like a good merchant who makes a profit everywhere, I want to bring you some merchandise from there as well.

8. I was walking alone like this as the day was already declining. My walk was along the shore, for I am somehow always in the habit of relieving my labours with such relaxations. A bowstring cannot bear to be kept constantly taut; it needs to be slackened a little from the notches if it is to be strung again, so as not to be useless to the archer or of no service when the time comes to use it. So I was walking; my feet carried me along, and my eyes were on the sea. It was not a pleasant sight, though at other times it is most pleasant, when it glows purple in a calm and plays sweetly and gently against the shores. But what was it like then? (For I gladly use the words of Scripture too.) "As a great wind was blowing" it was stirred up and roared. As usually happens in such commotions, some of the waves rose far out, gradually crested, then sank and broke on the shore; others struck the nearby rocks, were beaten back, and scattered into thin, foamy spray. Pebbles, seaweed, whelks and the lightest of the shellfish were thrown out and spat up there, and some were snatched back again as the wave retreated. But the rocks stood unshaken and unmoved, just as if nothing were disturbing them, except that they were struck by the waves.

9. From this, I know, I drew some profit for philosophy. Being the kind of man who applies everything to himself, especially if I happen to be

[?] dizzied by something that has happened, as I have been now, I did not pass over what I saw lightly, and the sight became a lesson to me. "Is not our life," I said, "and all human affairs a sea? There is much that is salty and unstable in them too. And are not the winds the temptations that assail us, and all the unexpected things?" I think the most wonderful David had this in mind when he said, "Save me, O Lord, for the waters have come in even to my soul," and, "Deliver me from the deep waters," and, "I came into the depths of the sea, and the storm overwhelmed me." Of those who are tempted, some seemed to me to be carried off like the lightest and most lifeless things, without resisting the assaults even a little, for they have no firmness in themselves, no weight of sober reasoning to stand against what assails them. Others seemed to be a rock, worthy of that Rock on which we stand and which we worship. These are the people who, using the reason of philosophy and having risen above the lowliness of the many, bear everything unshaken and unmoved, and either laugh at or pity those who are shaken: the first from philosophy, the second from love of humankind. They count it shameful to despise terrors while they are absent, or rather to think them no terrors at all, and then to be overcome when they come, and overcome by what? By things that pass away, as though they were lasting. They count it shameful to philosophize out of season and then appear unphilosophical when there is need, like someone who thinks himself the best of athletes without ever going down into the stadium, or a pilot who counts himself among the famous and is proud of his skill in fair weather, but lets go of the rudder in storms.

10. Once I had embarked on these reflections, I came also to another image, very fitting to the present circumstances. Perhaps you will think me an old man and a teller of tales if I tell it to you too; but it must be told, since I know that Scripture often uses such things to make its account clearer. There is a plant in a fable that flourishes when it is cut and contends against the iron; and, if I may speak paradoxically about a paradoxical thing,

[?]. So much for the fable and the free licence of invention. But to me the philosopher clearly seems to be something of this kind. He wins renown by his sufferings, makes painful things the material of virtue, and takes pride in adversities. He is neither lifted up by the weapons of righteousness on the right hand nor bent by those on the left; he remains the same though his circumstances do not, or rather he is found more approved, like gold in a furnace. Let us look at it this way. Is he of noble birth? He will match his blood with nobility of character, so as to be esteemed on two counts, both for his lineage and for what is seen in him. Is he lowborn in his statue and his clay (if indeed clay differs much from clay)? He will set against it the nobility of the mind, the nobility that each person shapes in himself for better or worse. The other kind, which is sown or recorded in writing, he will strike out as worthless and counterfeit. For birth is [?] threefold. The first kind began from above, and by it we are all equally noble, since we were made in the image of God. The second comes from the flesh, and I do not know whether anyone is noble by it, since it is made up of corruption. The third is known by vice or virtue, and we share in it more or less according as, I think, we either keep the image or corrupt it. This is the nobility that the truly wise man and philosopher will love. As for the fourth kind, the one found in documents and decrees, I will think it worth discussing when I accept the beauty that lies in paint and revere an ape that has been ordered to be a lion.

11. Is he young? He will act manfully against the passions, and will gain this from his youth: not to suffer what the young suffer, but to show an old man's prudence in a body at its prime. He will rejoice in the victory more than those crowned at Olympia, for he will win in a theatre shared by the whole world, and win a victory that cannot be bought. Is he declining into old age? He will not grow old in soul as well. He will accept dissolution as the appointed day of a necessary freedom, and will gladly pass on to what follows, where no one is too young or old, but all are perfect in spiritual age. Has he been given beauty? He will make beauty shine against beauty, that of the soul against that of the body. Has the bloom passed and left him unharmed? He turns to himself and does not even know that he is looked at. Is he ugly in what can be seen [?]

? Yet he is well-formed in what is hidden, like a blooming rose in a calyx that is neither blooming nor scented, the most fragrant thing within. Is he "fairer in beauty than the sons of men"? He gives no opportunity for his outward appearance to be gazed at, but turns the onlooker to the inner man. Is he in good health? He will use his health for the best: he will admonish, rebuke, speak freely, keep vigil, sleep on the ground, fast, reduce the material in himself, contemplate the things of earth and heaven, and with all zeal practise for death. Will he fall ill? He will fight; and if he is defeated, he will win by gaining release from fighting any more. Is he rich? He will make a philosophy of giving away his wealth, and will share what he has with the needy as the steward of what belongs to others, so that the one may benefit from the sharing and he himself may be gathered to God, having nothing but his cross and his body. Is he poor? He will be rich in God, and rich in laughing at those who possess, who are always acquiring and always poor because they need more, and who drink only to thirst the more.

12. Is he hungry? He will be fed along with the birds, whose life needs no sowing or ploughing. He will live with Elijah at the house of the widow of Zarephath: "The jar of oil shall not fail, and the jar of flour shall not run short." The one will flow forever, the other will yield richly, so that a hospitable widow may be honoured and may feed the one who feeds her. Is he thirsty [?]? Springs and rivers are his drink, a drink that neither intoxicates nor is measured out. If everything fails through drought, perhaps a torrent will give him water. Will he be cold? So was Paul; but for how long? There is even a garment of rock; let Job persuade you, when he says, "Because they had no shelter, they wrapped themselves in rock." Now consider with me the more perfect things. Will he be reviled? He will win by not reviling in return. Will he be persecuted? He will endure it. Will he be blasphemed? He will entreat. Will he be slandered? He will pray. Will he be struck on the right cheek? He will offer the other one too; if he had a third, he would offer that as well, the better to teach the one who strikes him patience, teaching by deed what he could not teach by word. Will he be reproached? So was Christ; he will be honoured by sharing in his suffering. Even if he is called a Samaritan, even if he is accused of having a demon, he will accept everything with God. Even if he suffers much, much will still be lacking: vinegar, gall, a crown of thorns, a sceptre of reed, a scarlet cloak, a cross, nails, robbers crucified with him, passers-by mock- [?]

-ing him. For one must have more of God by bearing more dishonour.

13. Nothing is harder to capture than philosophy, nothing harder to seize. Everything will give way before the philosopher does. "He is a wild ass in the desert," says Job, unbridled and free, laughing at the crowds of the city, not hearing the tax collector's complaint. He is a unicorn, a creature that is a law to itself. "Will it be willing to serve you? Will you tie it at a manger? Will it be brought under the yoke?" When he is shut out from everything on earth, wings like an eagle's have been prepared for him; he will return to the house of his master, he will fly up to God. Let me sum it up. Two beings are hard to master, God and an angel; and the third is the philosopher: immaterial in matter, uncircumscribed in a body, heavenly on earth, untouched by suffering amid sufferings, defeated in everything except his resolve, conquering by being conquered those who think they have the upper hand. Now that the discourse has drawn the philosopher for us, starting from where I said, come, let us examine our own affairs beside him (for I think that I too have the Spirit of God, even if in some of these things I am vulnerable and can be captured). Then, if those who hate and war against me find me defeated, they may at least pardon the attempt, if not the intention; but if they find me stronger and loftier than those who war against me, they may either be rid of their wickedness or devise some newer road of injustice, since the present one is held in contempt. So they will not be charged with folly as well as wickedness, for acting lawlessly to no purpose and not even knowing how to do the injustice they are so eager to do.

14. For how will they hurt me, even if they go to every length? Let us see how many ways a man can be wronged by men. Will they call me uneducated? I know one wisdom: to fear God. For "the beginning of wisdom is the fear of the Lord," and "the end of the matter, when all has been heard: fear God." So says Solomon, the wisest of men. Let them show that this is [?] unwise, and they win. As for the other wisdom, part of it I have run through, and the rest I pray and hope to gain, trusting in the Spirit. Will they charge me with poverty, my abundance? Would that I could strip off even these rags, so as to run naked through the thorns of life! Would that the heavy [?]

[?] this tunic as quickly as possible, so that I may have a lighter one. Will they call me a runaway from my homeland? How small-minded they are about us, truly insolent and hostile to strangers! Do I, my friends, have a homeland with fixed borders, I for whom every land is a homeland, and none is? And are you yourself not a stranger and a sojourner? I do not commend your settled dwelling, if that is how you live, lest you fall away from the true homeland, where we must lay up our citizenship. Will you reproach us with old age and sickliness? Is not all this a matter of matter and of nature? And, so that you may know one of my secrets, there is also what my mental labors have consumed, if I may boast a little. Nor are you, bursting with vigor and fattening your flesh, a pleasant sight to me. I wish some grey hair and pallor would bloom on you too, so that at least you might be believed to be wise and a philosopher.

15. What next? Will they depose me from thrones? Which thrones, then, did I ever mount gladly, either now or before? Do I count those who mount them blessed? Do you make them pleasant to me, when you mount them so unworthily? Did not what happened recently make my mind clear to you? Or was that too a kind of affectation, a way of testing desire? Crafty people might suspect some things about others, and say others, which are really true of themselves. What, then, of my contrition? What of the curses which I publicly called down on myself? What of my tears, and my becoming almost pitiable in your eyes, and hated for my resistance? Will they deprive me of precedence? When did any sensible person ever admire it, and who? As things are now, to escape it is, to my mind at least, the first mark of understanding. Because of it all our affairs are shaken and tossed about; because of it the ends of the world are filled with suspicion and with a kind of silent war that has not even a name; because of it we, who came into being from God, are in danger of belonging to men, and of casting off the great and new name. If only there were no precedence, no preference of place, no tyrannical privilege, so that we might be known by virtue alone! But as it is, this business of right and left and middle, of higher and lower, of walking ahead or walking alongside, has caused us many breakages to no purpose, has pushed many into the pit, and has led them away to the place of the goats; and not only those below, but now even the shepherds, who, though they are teachers of Israel, did not know these things.

[?] of varied things, but the work is wholly of the mind, and the ascent is through contemplation. Before this altar I will present myself; on this I will offer acceptable gifts, sacrifice and offering and whole burnt offerings, as much better than those now brought as truth is better than shadow. It is about this, I think, that the great David also speaks with wisdom when he says: "And I will go in to the altar of God, who gladdens my spiritual youth." From this altar no one who wishes to will lead me away. Will they drive me out of the city? But not out of the city that lies above. Let those who hate us manage that, and then they will truly have made war; but as long as they cannot, they are pelting us with raindrops, or striking at the breezes, or playing at dreams. That is how I see their war. Will they strip me of wealth? What wealth? If it is mine, let them cut off [?] even what I have never laid hands on. If it is the Church's, that is what the whole war is about: it is for this that the thief covets the money-box and betrays God for thirty pieces of silver, the most dreadful thing of all. For it is not the one betrayed but the betrayer who is worth so little.

17. Will they shut me out of houses? Cut off my luxuries? Turn my friends against me? Oh yes, as you see, I have been a burden to a great many people, even though they invited me (for I will not be ungrateful); and if I was a burden, it was rather by sparing them than by accepting their hospitality. The reason is this: a certain house gave us rest, pious and God-loving, like that of the Shunammite woman for Elisha, kin to us in body and kin in spirit, generous in every way. With them this people too was planted, still keeping its persecuted piety in secret, not without fear or danger. May the Lord repay them in the day of recompense! But if we pursue luxury, may those who hate us revel in triumph over us; for I could call down no greater curse on myself. As for my friends, some, I know well, will flee from us even though they suffer no harm themselves (for being wronged along with someone makes one share their pain as well); by others we have already been trained to bear being despised. For of my friends and neighbors, some openly drew near against me and took their stand, while others, most painful of all [?], stood far off, and on this night all of them took offense. Peter too all but denied me; and perhaps he does not even weep bitterly to heal his sin.

[Critical notes:] Ἡ ἀνάβασις ("the ascent"): lacking in Or. 1 [?]. Μὴ τοῦτο: so Reg. [?]; τοῦτο is lacking in [?] the inferior manuscripts. Reg. [?] reads πλεῖστον.

18. It seems I alone am bold and full of daring; I alone am hopeful in the midst of terrors; I alone am steadfast [?], at once exposed in public and despised in private, and known to East and West for being warred against. What madness! "Though an army encamp against me, my heart shall not fear; though war rise up against me, in this I will hope." So far am I from thinking anything in the present situation fearful that, setting aside my own case, I mourn for those who have grieved me. Members of Christ once, members precious to me, even if now corrupted, members of this flock which you all but betrayed even before it was gathered: how were you torn apart, and how did you tear others apart, like calves let loose from their tethers? How did you raise up altar against altar? How did you suddenly become a desolation? How have you both brought death on yourselves by the schism and made us grieve? How did you abuse the simplicity of shepherds to scatter the flock? For I do not blame them for their inexperience, but I will accuse you of wickedness. "Who will help you in your ruin, O Israel?" What healing remedy shall I find? What bandage? How shall I join together what has been torn apart [?]? With what tears, what words, what prayers shall I heal the fracture? Or perhaps in this way?

19. Holy Trinity, worshipful and perfect, rightly brought together and revered by us, yours is the work, yours the achievement. May you restore these men to us again, having been parted from us only so far as to be taught concord by the separation; and in return for our toils here may you grant us the heavenly things that know no strife. Of these the first and greatest is to be illumined by you more perfectly and more purely, so as to understand how the same God is both conceived as a Monad and found to be a Trinity; how the Unbegotten, the Begotten and the Proceeding are one nature, three properties, one God, who is over all, through all and in all; neither exceeding himself, nor changing place, nor diminished, nor divided; in part comprehended now, in part still sought, and perhaps one day to be comprehended, as far as that is possible, by those who here have sought well through their life and contemplation. To him be all glory, honor and might forever. Amen.
